h1: Running the brewpub kitchen yourself or leasing it out
title: Brewpub Kitchen: Run It or Lease It | Craft Beer School
desc: Should a brewpub run its own kitchen or lease it to an operator? The numbers, the risks and the questions to ask before you decide.
teaser: The kitchen can make or break a brewpub. Running it and leasing it out are both honest options, with different risks.
standfirst: Many brewpub owners know beer and not food. The choice between running the kitchen yourself or leasing it to an operator changes your margin, your control and your workload. Here is how to compare the two.
sections: Two models, two sets of risks

If you run the kitchen yourself, you hire the chef, buy the food and take all the profit or loss. If you lease it, an operator pays you rent or a share of sales and carries the food costs. Neither is better in general. Each fits a different owner.

Run it yourself if you have, or can hire, a strong kitchen manager and you want control of the guest experience. Lease it if food is not your skill and you would rather focus on beer. Our guide to laying out a brewpub shows how the kitchen shapes the whole floor plan, whichever model you choose.

Food margins depend on menu, wastage and portion control. Use your own figures, not a rule of thumb. Here is a method with made up numbers: if a plate sells for ₹400 before tax and its ingredients cost ₹140, the ingredient cost is 35% and the gross margin is 65%. Then subtract wages, gas, packaging, wastage and repairs. What remains is much smaller than the gross margin, which surprises many first-time owners.

A leased kitchen replaces that whole calculation with a rent or a revenue share. Your income is steadier but capped. Run the same menu through both models on a spreadsheet and compare the annual figure after tax and after the staff you would have to hire.
What a lease needs to say

A kitchen lease is a business contract, so use a lawyer. Questions to settle:

  • Rent: fixed, a share of sales or a mix?
  • Menu control: who decides the menu, the prices and the brand standards?
  • Beer pairing: must the operator use your beers in dishes and recommend them?
  • Food safety: who holds the licence, who pays for audits and what happens after a failed inspection?
  • Utilities, repairs and equipment: who pays for what?
  • Exit: what is the notice period? Who owns the equipment at the end?

Food licensing in India is separate from the alcohol licence and rules differ by state. Check both before signing.

A kitchen is the biggest wage block in many brewpubs. Plan for a head cook, line cooks, a dishwasher and someone to cover weekly offs and sick days, since a kitchen that closes mid-service costs more than the wage it saves. Long split shifts and late nights make retention hard, so budget for training and a realistic roster. Our guide to monthly payroll for a brewpub team shows how the total builds up.

Guests do not separate the beer from the food. A slow kitchen or a bad plate lowers the score for the whole pub. If you lease, set service standards in the contract: ticket times, hygiene checks and a say over the menu. Visit often, eat there and ask regulars what they think.

If you run it yourself, you own all of these problems and all of the upside. That includes the 11 pm dosa order that nobody planned for.

The best brewpub kitchens cook with the beer as well as serve it: beer-battered fish, a stout in a stew, a lager cheese sauce or a spent grain flatbread. A tied operator may do this well. A third-party tenant may not care. If pairing is part of your idea, make it a clause. Then train the staff to talk about it.

Do not force it where it does not fit. A good plate beside a good beer matters more than a clever menu line.

Answer five questions with a score from 1 to 5.

  1. Do you have a kitchen manager you trust?
  2. Can you fund the extra working capital and equipment?
  3. Do you want to spend your time on food?
  4. Is the food a key part of the guest's reason to visit?
  5. Can you find a tenant whose brand fits yours?

If questions one to three score high, run it. If the third scores low and the fifth high, lease it. If both score low, simplify the menu and review again in six months. Our guide to leasing space for a brewpub covers the other side of the table. Our guide to happy hour pricing shows how the bar and kitchen margin interact.
Where to learn the money side

Whichever model you choose, you need to read a kitchen margin, a stock count and a cash plan with confidence. That commercial skill set is what the Brewery Business Management course teaches, with real worked examples for brewery and brewpub owners.
faqs: Is it cheaper to lease a brewpub kitchen?
It lowers your risk and your capital, but it also caps your income. Compare the annual figure from both models on a spreadsheet using your own costs.
Who holds the food licence in a leased kitchen?
That is set in the lease and by state rules. Settle it in writing and check with a lawyer or licensing adviser.
Can a tenant cook with my beer?
Yes, if you write it into the lease and give the kitchen team training. Many tenants will not do it unless asked.
